# Results — Study 946 (Distribution is not Return) on the real monthly tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Fifteen listed income ETFs are
ranked each month by their **trailing-12-month distribution rate**, reconstructed from the
gap between the total-return tape (`yfinance`, `auto_adjust=True`) and the price-only tape
(`auto_adjust=False`). The rank formed at the close of month `t` is held through month
`t+1` — **one execution lag, and it is the only lag in the study**. The same equal-weight
top-tercile-minus-bottom-tercile sort is then scored against three different left-hand
sides: next month's payout, next month's **price-only** return, and next month's **total**
return. Cash leg = BIL total return; risk benchmark = SPY total return. As-of
**2026-06-30** (the partial current month is dropped).*

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | Held months | Fingerprints (of **returns**) |
|---|---|--:|---|
| 15 income ETFs + SPY (bench) + BIL (cash), two tapes each | daily 2003-01-02 → 2026-06-30; held months 2013-11-30 → 2026-06-30 | 152 | total-return `ac334d204e26` · price-only `b94d79082051` |

The stamp fingerprints **returns, not price levels**, and that is deliberate: `yfinance`'s
`auto_adjust=True` back-adjusts the *entire* history every time a new distribution lands, so
a level fingerprint of the total-return tape drifts on every re-fetch without a single
return changing (the shared `studies/_cache` is refreshed by whichever study fetches last).
Returns are invariant to that rescale, so this stamp reproduces — and still moves the moment
one observation genuinely changes. See `data.returns_fingerprint` and its test.

Cross-section width 6 → 15 funds (tercile size *k* = 2 → 5). The panel starts in
2013-11 because that is the first month with six funds carrying twelve months of payout
history.

The reconstruction lands on the marketed numbers (QYLD ~12.8%, JEPI ~8.3%, SCHD ~3.7%,
NOBL ~2.2%), which is the check that the TR/PR gap really is the distribution. Read the
last two columns as a pair: every fund above 6% has a **negative or near-zero price CAGR**
and every fund below 4% has a strongly positive one, while the *total*-return column is
scrambled with respect to payout.

## Fama-MacBeth — what does the payout rank actually predict?

Cross-sectionally z-scored trailing payout rate at `t` → month `t+1`'s outcome; time-series
mean of 152 monthly slopes, Newey-West 6 lags.

| Left-hand side | bps/month per 1 sd of payout rate | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| next month's **payout** | **+24.6** | **+11.27** |
| next month's **price-only** return | **−28.1** | **−3.84** |
| next month's **TOTAL** return | −3.5 | −0.48 |

The payout is one of the most forecastable quantities on the desk. The price path is
forecastable too — downwards, and *because* of the payout, since the price leg is the total
leg minus the payout leg by construction. The thing an investor is buying — total return —
is not forecastable at all.

**How strong is that "not at all"?** It is a *bounded* null, not a precise zero. The
tercile spread's block-bootstrap CI is [−47.2, +10.4] bps/month, i.e. **[−5.67%, +1.25%] a
year**. So the tape rules out the marketed reading — ranking on payout buys you more than
about **+1.25%/yr** of extra total return — with reasonable confidence, and rules out
essentially *nothing* on the downside: a genuine 4%/yr penalty for holding the fat payers
sits comfortably inside the interval. The honest statement is "no evidence the sticker buys
you anything", not "proof it costs you nothing".

## The tercile sort — high payout minus low payout

Equal-weight top tercile minus bottom tercile, monthly rebalance, one-month lag.

| Leg | bps/month | HAC *t* | Bootstrap 95% CI (bps) | P(>0) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **payout** (`hml_d`) | **+51.6** | **+10.27** | [+42.4, +60.5] | 1.000 |
| **price-only** return (`hml_p`) | **−69.9** | **−4.53** | [−100.5, −40.4] | 0.000 |
| **TOTAL** return (`hml`) | −18.3 | −1.24 | [−47.2, +10.4] | 0.102 |

Average trailing payout at formation: **9.92%** on the high leg, **2.87%** on the low leg —
a **7.05 pp** spread. Bootstrap: 2,000 draws, 6-month moving blocks.

### Read the three rows as one row: the price leg is an identity

Because the payout is *defined* as the total/price gap, the three legs are not three
experiments. They satisfy

> `hml_price ≡ hml_total − hml_payout`

to machine precision: −69.9 bps versus −18.3 − 51.6 = −69.9 bps, month-by-month correlation
**0.99995** (printed as an `IDENTITY CHECK` line by `verify.py`, asserted in the tests). So
the *t* = −4.53 on "NAV erosion" is **not independent evidence**; it is the
payout-persistence *t* carried over once the total-return leg contributes nothing. What the
tape actually supplies is two things — a strongly forecastable payout (*t* = +11.3) and a
total-return null — and the erosion follows by arithmetic. Everything below is written that
way, and the Signal stamp is claimed on that pair, not on the erosion *t* twice over.

**Give-back ratio = 1.36.** For every extra basis point of distribution the high-payout leg
pays out, 1.36 bps come off its quoted price. It is emphatically not 0 (the free-money
reading). But note what the same identity implies: give-back = 1 − `hml_total`/`hml_payout`,
so the **distance from a clean 1.00 is exactly the total-return leg** — and that leg carries
*t* = −1.24. The point estimate is above one; the tape does **not** support the claim that
the fat payers erode *more* than they distribute. Read 1.36 as "1, and no evidence of
better".

## Excess-of-cash race (every leg minus BIL) and the CAPM control

| Arm | Excess Sharpe | mean (bps/mo) | vol | HAC *t* | max DD | total-return CAGR |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| High-payout tercile | +0.737 | +62.6 | 10.2% | +2.96 | −20.1% | **+9.06%** |
| Low-payout tercile | +0.731 | +80.9 | 13.3% | +3.58 | −23.3% | **+11.07%** |
| SPY (benchmark) | **+0.862** | +104.4 | 14.5% | +4.27 | −24.4% | **+14.02%** |

| CAPM (excess-of-cash on SPY excess-of-cash) | α (bps/mo) | HAC *t*(α) | β | R² |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| High-payout leg | −5.3 | −0.59 | +0.650 | 0.859 |
| Low-payout leg | −2.5 | −0.17 | +0.798 | 0.764 |
| High minus low | −2.8 | −0.18 | −0.148 | 0.076 |

The high-payout leg is a **0.65-beta equity position with no alpha**. Its slightly better
Sharpe than the low-payout leg is a volatility artefact, and both trail SPY. There is no
alpha on either side of the sort, and none in the spread.

## Robustness — two eras (split 2020-06-30, the income-ETF boom line)

| Era | n | payout | **price** (*t*) | **TOTAL** (*t*) | give-back | CAPM α (*t*) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2013-11 → 2020-06 | 80 | +31.2 | **−51.7** (−3.28) | −20.6 (−1.31) | 1.65 | −0.8 (−0.06) |
| 2020-07 → 2026-06 | 72 | +74.3 | **−90.3** (−3.46) | −15.7 (−0.61) | 1.22 | −4.9 (−0.18) |

The erosion clears |*t*| = 3 in **both** halves and roughly doubles as the payouts
themselves doubled. The total-return leg is dead in both halves. This is a mechanical
identity holding across regimes, not a regime effect.

## Robustness — sort width, the corporate-action guard, the universe

| Variant | price (*t*) | TOTAL (*t*) |
|---|--:|--:|
| tercile (frac 1/3) — headline | −69.9 (−4.53) | −18.3 (−1.24) |
| quintile-ish (frac 0.20) | −67.6 (−4.20) | −8.4 (−0.54) |
| wide sort (frac 0.40) | −65.0 (−4.54) | −17.2 (−1.23) |
| **no** corporate-action guard — *the live-tradable read* | −57.0 (−2.79) | −5.4 (−0.26) |
| guard 0.40 instead of 0.50 | −69.9 (−4.53) | −18.3 (−1.24) |
| NUSI dropped outright | −68.0 (−5.21) | −20.4 (−1.61) |
| **option-income cohort only** (9 funds, 74 mo from 2020-05) | −50.8 (−1.93) | +7.2 (+0.30) |

Three honest reads here. First, **the guard is a hindsight filter and is named as one**: it
drops a fund-month by looking at the return of the very month being predicted, so a fund
leaves the sort formed at *t* because of what its *t+1* print turns out to be. No live
trader could run it. It fires **exactly once** in the whole panel (NUSI, 2025-02 — an
unadjusted 1-for-2 reverse split Yahoo! applied to neither tape), and the row to read if you
object to it on principle is the **no-guard** row: the price leg is −57.0 (*t* = −2.79), the
total leg is −5.4 (*t* = −0.26), and neither stamp moves. Deleting NUSI outright — no
hindsight anywhere — gives −68.0 (*t* = −5.21) and −20.4 (*t* = −1.61).

Second, the erosion result is **insensitive** to sort width, to the guard threshold and to
removing the one broken fund. Third, inside the **option-income cohort alone** —
nine buy-write/derivative-income wrappers over only 74 months — the erosion drops to
*t* = −1.93 and the total-return leg turns (insignificantly) positive. Part of the
headline erosion *magnitude* is therefore *cross-cohort* (buy-write wrappers versus
dividend-equity funds), not a within-cohort law; the within-cohort window is too short and
too narrow to settle the magnitude either way.

What does **not** soften inside the cohort is the pair the Signal stamp actually rests on.
Within those nine wrappers the payout rank still forecasts the next payout at +28.4 bps/sd,
HAC *t* = **+10.63** (74 months), and still forecasts total return not at all (+6.6 bps/sd,
*t* = +0.60). The payout leg is era-stable too: Fama-MacBeth *t* = +12.6 in the first era and
+32.7 in the second. The erosion magnitude is the cross-cohort part; the two measured facts
are not.

## Cost × borrow sweep on the tradable (high-minus-low) leg

One-way name turnover: **0.049/month** on the high leg, **0.043** on the low leg — a
low-turnover sort, so friction is small. Borrow on the short leg is an **ASSUMPTION**
(not tape) and is swept.

| One-way cost | Borrow (bps/yr) | TOTAL (bps/mo) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 (gross) | 0 | −18.3 | −1.24 |
| 5 | 50 | −22.9 | −1.56 |
| 5 | 100 | −27.1 | −1.84 |
| 10 | 100 | −27.6 | −1.87 |
| 25 | 200 | −37.3 | −2.52 |

Costs cannot rescue the trade: the spread is already negative and insignificant gross, and
friction only pushes it further into "short the high payers" territory — which is a
different (and, at *t* = −1.24 gross, unfounded) claim.

## Synthetic control (offline; machinery proof — never supports the stamp)

| World | FM total (*t*) | FM price (*t*) | FM payout (*t*) | give-back |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **null**, `signal_strength=0` (pure return of capital) | +0.3 (+0.10) | −28.8 (−8.80) | +29.5 (+122.1) | 0.99 |
| **planted**, `signal_strength=1` (a real yield→return link) | **+30.2 (+9.20)** | +0.9 (+0.27) | +29.5 (+122.1) | −0.02 |

The planted slope was **+30.0 bps/sd** and the estimator recovered **+30.2**. On the null it
reads **+0.3 bps (t = +0.10)**, with the erosion identity recovered at a give-back of 0.99.
Across 8 seeds the null's total-return slope averages **−2.4 bps (sd 3.1)** and never
exceeds 20 bps. A separate **beta-confound** world (`beta_slope=0.5`, no alpha) produces a
raw high-minus-low of −18.1 bps that the CAPM control correctly reduces to α = −1.2 bps
(*t* = −0.18) at β = −1.10 — so the real-tape α of −2.8 bps is a genuine zero, not an
un-modelled beta.

## Verdict

- **Signal — Real**, and stated precisely, because the arithmetic does a lot of the work.
  The tape supplies **two** facts, not three. (1) The trailing payout rate forecasts
  **next month's payout** with *t* = **+11.3** (+24.6 bps/sd) — sticky payout policy, real
  and strongly measured on the real tape, era-stable, and the one estimate here that is not
  a restatement of another. (2) It forecasts **total return not at all**: −18.3 bps/mo,
  *t* = −1.24, bootstrap CI [−47.2, +10.4] bps/mo = **[−5.67%, +1.25%] per year**, CAPM
  α = −2.8 bps (*t* = −0.18). The famous third fact — the **−69.9 bps/mo NAV erosion**,
  *t* = −4.53 — is **an identity given the first two** (`hml_price ≡ hml_total −
  hml_payout`, correlation 0.99995), so it is reported as arithmetic, never as independent
  confirmation. On that pair the claim under test survives on the real tape: what the
  distribution rate ranks is the cash coming out, not the money coming in. Four caveats
  travel with it. The null is **bounded, not precise** — it kills the marketed reading above
  ~+1.25%/yr and rules out nothing on the downside. The give-back of **1.36** is "1.00 plus
  an insignificant total-return leg", so *more*-than-one-for-one erosion is a point estimate
  and not a finding. The erosion magnitude is partly **cross-cohort** (it softens to
  *t* = −1.93 inside the nine option-income wrappers over their 74 common months). And the
  universe is **survivorship-selected** — these are the income ETFs that gathered assets and
  stayed listed, and the sort silently skips any fund without a next-month print — so the
  high-payout leg's total return is an upper bound. NUSI itself stopped trading in July
  2026, one month after the as-of.
- **Tradability — Mirage.** There is nothing to bank. The one tradable expression of the
  finding — long low-payout, short high-payout — earns +18.3 bps/mo **gross** with
  *t* = 1.24 and a bootstrap CI straddling zero, and the short leg pays a borrow fee that
  only makes it worse. The long-only reading is no better: the high-payout tercile returns
  **+9.06%/yr** against the low-payout tercile's **+11.07%** and SPY's **+14.02%**, at an
  excess-of-cash Sharpe of 0.737 versus SPY's 0.862, with a CAPM α of −5.3 bps/mo
  (*t* = −0.59) on a β of 0.65. The distribution rate is a **transparency tool**, not a
  signal: it tells you where the cash is coming from, and it tells you nothing about how
  much you will end up with.
